findings.text: Now that [heading] means a CommonMark heading, the heading `init` writes from a folder name is parsed as CommonMark, so a name holding Markdown syntax does not come out as written: `*shop*` becomes emphasis, a name ending in ` #` loses it as a closing sequence, and a `\` before punctuation escapes it on Unix. No rule says whether `init` writes such a name as it is or escapes it, or whether the heading's text still equals the name in those cases; all three Examples rows use names without such characters.
findings.reason: the rule says what is written, the name as it is; how it renders changes neither lint nor diff, and the case is older than this amendment

findings.text: part_kinds says the parts are the ones lint already tells apart. The amendment changes what lint tells apart: a setext-underlined line is now a heading and opens a section, a heading in a list item or block quote is now text, and a table after a rule's Examples table is now prose. So the parts that manifest and diff split an element into change too. baseline.parts.split marks no [heading] or [table], and part_kinds is prose, so neither is among the changed-through elements or the candidates.
findings.reason: the amendment states how lint already reads Markdown and changes no reading; part_kinds follows lint by its Rationale, as before

findings.text: The new body of lint.references.marked says a link inside a rule block is written `[text](destination)`, but CommonMark, by which [link] is now defined, recognises no link inside a fenced block. So no rule says whether other link forms there are links or term marks: `[text](destination "title")`, `[text](<destination with spaces>)`, `[text][label]`, or `[text]` matching a link reference definition.

The new body of lint.references.marked decides what a term mark is: a `[…]` directly followed by `(` is a link and no mark, and `[text][label]` is two marks. This changes lint.references.term, since `[rest of it](notes.md)` used to be a mark that does not resolve (error) and now gives nothing, and lint.undecided.term, since a link to an open term's name is no longer a mark. Neither rule is among the candidates or listed as changed through, and neither has an Examples row for a link.

What counts as a term mark in a rule block is decided only in the body of a lint feature. system.term still says only "marked as `[term]` in a rule block". baseline reads term marks for `dependencies` ("every glossary entry whose term its rule block marks") and for baseline.diff.undecided (marks of an open term), and nothing at system level tells it that `[spec tree](notes.md)` marks nothing or that `[spec tree][tree]` marks two terms.

The body of lint.references.marked calls a `[` whose `]` is directly followed by `(` a "link", but system.link means a CommonMark link with no Deviations. CommonMark finds no links inside a fenced block, and `[a](b c)` is no CommonMark link. lint's Rationale says such departures are stated in a term's Deviations, and here none is.

system.examples-table, touched by this amendment, still defines every Examples table as having a `provided` column. lint.examples.provided-column reports an error for a `provided` column on a rule without a guard (row `findings`, `provided`, `outcome` with guarded "no"), so an unguarded rule's table cannot both meet the definition and pass lint.

system.term now says a term is also marked in a "Represents" field. So baseline.diff.undecided now lists a contract element whose Represents field marks an open term as not to be built, and coherence.verify.undecided reports it "undecided". But lint.undecided.term only asks about a mark in a rule block, so lint reports nothing for that open mark. The lint.undecided Goal is that every place the tree leaves undecided is reported.

The two rules now count only an open term's marks in an element's rule block, and their new rows make a contract element whose "Represents" field marks an open term to be built, with nothing reported for it. The contract still describes `undecided`, the "Not to be built:" line and the `undecided` problem kind by any "mark of an open term" ("an element ... marks an open term" in `verification`), which a "Represents" field's mark is, so for that contract element the contract makes it not to be built and reported.

lint.run.order orders findings "then kind" without saying how kinds compare: by their names byte by byte, or in the order the findings contract lists its members. Row 2 holds under both readings, but they disagree elsewhere, such as identifier-malformed against identifier-duplicate on one line, so two builds can order the same findings differently.
